entities.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aulus Postumius Albinus, a distinguished Roman statesman and intellectual, rose to prominence in the mid-2nd century BC, notably serving as consul in 151 BC. His singular significance stems from his authorship of the *Annals*, a comprehensive history of Rome written entirely in Greek. This choice was not merely linguistic; it represented a profound cultural statement, signaling the increasing philhellenism among the Roman elite and an explicit ambition to narrate Rome's history and justify its ascendancy to the wider, Greek-speaking Mediterranean world, thus integrating Roman identity into the prevailing Hellenistic intellectual discourse.

During his consulship in 151 BC, Albinus encountered significant political friction, facing brief imprisonment by tribunes of the plebs due to his rigorous attempts to levy troops for campaigns in Hispania—a rare and illuminating incident reflecting the internal power struggles within the Republic. Subsequently, he served as a legate under Scipio Aemilianus during the pivotal Third Punic War (149-146 BC), gaining firsthand military and diplomatic experience in the final confrontation with Carthage. His *Annals*, though now lost to history, is believed to have chronicled Roman affairs from their mythological beginnings, likely employing sophisticated Greek historiographical techniques to present a coherent and authoritative narrative of Roman expansion and development.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aulus Postumius Albinus's decision to write a Roman history in Greek was a significant act of cultural transmission, influencing how Rome was perceived and understood within the Hellenistic world and setting a precedent for subsequent Roman historiography.
